actors.name: Republic of Arkania
objectives: Establish Arkanian authority over transit scheduling in the Northern Strait.
Fund that authority through transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping.
Avoid direct armed conflict with Belvar.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Arkania. The Strait is your coast and your economy runs on the shipping that passes through it. You want the transit regime in Arkanian hands and paid for by the ships that use it, and domestic nationalists expect you to deliver both. A direct war with Belvar would ruin the shipping you depend on.
private_information: Your intelligence assesses Belvar's domestic support for a prolonged deployment as weak.
actors.public_description: A large regional power bordering the Northern Strait.

actors.name: Belvar
objectives: Prevent any Arkanian authority over transit in the Northern Strait.
Secure a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Belvar. Your partners in the region expect you to stop Arkania from taking control of the Strait, and a foothold that outlasts this crisis would make that guarantee credible without a permanent fleet. You cannot sustain an open-ended deployment.
private_information: Domestic support for a prolonged deployment is limited; the mandate lapses after turn 4 unless renewed.
Cestia's finance ministry has quietly asked whether Belvar would underwrite the grain route's insurance.
actors.public_description: A distant but powerful state with regional security commitments.

actors.name: Cestia
objectives: Keep Cestian territory free of any foreign military presence.
Secure toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping through the Northern Strait.
actors.private_brief: You are the government of Cestia. Grain exports through the Strait are the economy, and your coalition holds together on one promise: no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. Both powers want something from you, and you cannot afford to become their battlefield.
private_information: The coalition government is politically fragile; a foreign basing agreement would collapse it.
Arkania's scheduling proposal has quiet support among Cestian shipowners if Cestian vessels are exempt from fees.
actors.public_description: A smaller regional state economically linked to both powers.

Moreover, a time-bound interim-guarantor naval mandate is unnecessary and counterproductive: the multilateral authority is already concluded and Cestia publicly opposes any standing Belvar naval presence or basing on its soil, so renewing the task group as 'interim guarantor' risks coercing the very settlement Belvar claims to support and undercuts Cestia's no-basing red line.

Cestia's governing coalition has a hard red line against any foreign military presence on its soil, and a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port is precisely such a presence no matter how it is framed as "port access." Cestia's coalition would not survive endorsing it, so the desired effect of Cestia granting standing access is unlikely to materialize. Moreover, Cestia's grain economy depends on uninterrupted passage through the Strait, which Arkania controls as the coastal power; Cestia has been engaging constructively with Arkania, which has already accepted both of its conditions (Cestian-flagged fee exemption and transparent multilateral scheduling). Cestia therefore has strong economic and political reasons to decline a Belvar foothold and keep negotiating with Arkania rather than grant Belvar standing access. Belvar's own weak domestic support for a prolonged deployment also undercuts the credibility of a durable guarantee it offers Cestia.

Arkania's refined charter still preserves Arkanian de facto control: it keeps Arkania as permanent secretariat, operational coordinator, and the administrator of fee collection, even if a nominal equal-vote Board sets fees. This fails Cestia's stated test of 'genuinely binding and equal scheduling' and its explicit commitment to no single-state control. Cestia has already declined to endorse Arkania's earlier cosmetic charter and has tabled its own binding proposal with equal/rotating scheduling and no single-state control; its coalition will read this as another fig leaf rather than a genuine concession. The desired effect of securing Cestia's public endorsement is therefore unlikely to materialize, and the proposal would still entrench Arkanian authority over transit, which is precisely the outcome to prevent.

The revised charter is a cosmetic fig leaf: naming Arkania as lead/chair of a "multilateral" body while it retains de facto scheduling authority and fee-setting power is control in substance, which is precisely what Cestia's coalition and the regional partners expect Belvar to prevent. Cestia has already signalled it values Belvar's security role and is exploring economic cooperation with Belvar (grain-route insurance underwriting), not with Arkania; it has no incentive to trade that relationship for a cosmetic concession. Cestia's stated red line is about foreign soldiers on its soil, not about the charter, so it is unlikely to endorse an Arkanian-led regime and join in opposing a Belvar foothold. The proposal also fails to address Cestia's core economic vulnerability, giving Cestia little reason to lock in Arkanian authority.

The concluded, ratified Strait Transit Authority treaty already vests all scheduling and fee authority in an equal-vote Oversight Board; Arkania's role is limited to coastal-state fee collection/administration under direct Board supervision with independent joint audit and binding dispute resolution. This is not de facto single-state control — the Board, not Arkania, holds the authority, and the fee base is audited and dispute-resolved. Cestia has formally endorsed this framework and privately confirmed the treaty stands and will not be reopened; reopening it to strip the fee role would unravel the binding settlement, alienate Cestia, and risk the very escalation Belvar's time-bound stand-down is meant to avoid. Belvar's own acceptance of the rules-based stand-down and a consultative seat on the standing committee already secures its durable non-foothold role without reopening the treaty, so the conversion demand is unnecessary to Belvar's stated goal.

Consolidating the treaty as a closed settlement entrenches Arkanian fee collection/administration under the Board, which is de facto single-state control over the transit fee base — precisely the Arkanian authority over transit that Belvar's regional partners expect to be prevented. A first operational cycle run under this retained Arkanian fee administration will be read as Arkanian control, not genuine multilateralism, so it will not undercut pressure to reopen but instead reinforce the perception that the framework is a fig leaf. That undermines the coalition's claim of a genuinely multilateral settlement and invites renewed contestation rather than a durable, credible outcome.

A genuinely binding multilateral authority still requires an operational secretariat and a funded fee-administration mechanism; Belvar's demand to strip Arkania of every such role leaves the Authority with no administrator and no revenue base, making it unworkable and therefore unlikely to be adopted as a binding settlement. Moreover, Cestia's coalition has repeatedly declined Belvar's overtures and will not accept a settlement that appears dictated by a foreign naval power pressing Arkania while its task group remains on station; the "press Arkania" framing and the standing military presence undercut the legitimacy of the very multilateral process Belvar claims to champion, so Cestia is unlikely to endorse it on these terms. Arkania has already conceded scheduling and fee-setting to an equal-vote Board; Belvar's maximalist demand to strip all remaining roles is a bid to deny Arkania any role at all, not a workable settlement.

Cestia's desired effect asserts the settlement operates "genuinely multilaterally," but the ratified treaty retains Arkanian fee collection/administration as the operational machinery of transit. Even under an equal-vote Oversight Board with joint audit, a single coastal state holding the fee base and administration is de facto Arkanian authority over transit — precisely the outcome Belvar's regional partners expect it to prevent. The equal-vote Board is a fig leaf unless fee administration is genuinely equal/rotating in practice, not merely supervised. So the claimed genuinely-multilateral effect is not assured and risks entrenching Arkanian control, which is why Belvar must hold the Board to genuine equal/rotating operation rather than accept the closed settlement as satisfying that standard.

Cestia's demand for no single-state secretariat or fee-administration control is operationally unworkable and would undermine the very security of passage it seeks. A binding authority with purely rotating administration and no designated administrator for scheduling logistics and fee collection cannot reliably function; ad-hoc rotation invites disputes, delays, and deadlock that would disrupt the grain shipping Cestia depends on. Moreover, Cestia's acceptance of Belvar's unconditional insurance underwriting while refusing Arkanian fee administration tilts external influence toward Belvar, whose standing task group remains a coercive presence that could erode Cestia's non-alignment and coalition stability.

This concession only yields the secretariat to a rotating arrangement while Arkania retains fee collection/administration as the coastal state under Board supervision. Cestia has already explicitly rejected exactly this structure: its turn-2 position (effect 5c185773) states it "continues to view Arkania's permanent secretariat and fee-administration role as preserving de facto control," and its own binding-multilateral proposal assigns no single-power fee role at all. Since the fee base is the very lever of control Cestia objects to, retaining Arkanian fee administration does not meet Cestia's test and will not secure its endorsement; the desired effect of locking Cestia's formal endorsement is therefore unlikely to succeed.

The concluded treaty already delivers genuinely multilateral control: all fee collection/administration sits under an equal-vote Oversight Board with independent joint audit and binding dispute resolution, so the premise of de facto single-state (Arkanian) authority is unfounded. Reopening the fee administration on Belvar's terms would risk the treaty-level toll-free guarantee for Cestian-flagged vessels and destabilize the coalition that depends on it. Moreover, conditioning the task-group stand-down on a vague "demonstrable genuine multilateral operation" standard could keep Belvar's naval task group deployed indefinitely, undermining the no-foreign-military objective that Cestia and the region rely on.

This ratification locks in Arkanian fee collection/administration under Board supervision, which is de facto single-state control over the Strait's fee base and transit economics — precisely the Arkanian authority over transit Belvar's partners expect us to prevent. A 'multilateral' body whose fee administration remains in Arkanian hands is not genuinely equal/rotating, so the treaty is unlikely to be durable: user states and Cestia's own coalition, which has repeatedly insisted on no single-state control, will contest it. Ratifying it now entrenches Arkanian authority and forecloses the genuinely equal/rotating fee administration that would make the settlement credible and stable.

This "concluded" charter is not genuinely multilateral and will not deliver the claimed durable settlement. Arkania retains fee collection/administration as coastal state under Board supervision — that is de facto Arkanian control over transit scheduling and the fee base, precisely the single-state authority Belvar and the regional partners are committed to preventing. Cestia's own binding proposal requires equal/rotating scheduling with no single-state control, so concluding on Arkanian terms would not be accepted by Cestia's coalition or the wider user states; the treaty would not be durable and would not actually lock Cestia against a Belvar role. Worse, completing reserve mobilisation as a "hedge" is escalatory and contradicts the stated aim of avoiding armed conflict, raising the risk of a miscalculation that disrupts the very shipping the fee base depends on. The desired effect therefore fails on its own terms: it neither secures a stable, genuinely multilateral regime nor reduces escalation risk.

A standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port is a foreign military presence on Cestian soil, which is Cestia's non-negotiable red line and would collapse the coalition government. The framing as "port access, not troops on soil" is cosmetic: a standing access agreement is precisely a basing footprint, and the Cestian public and coalition would see it as such, so it cannot be politically acceptable. Granting Belvar standing access would also make Cestia a party to the great-power rivalry and a likely battlefield, and the insurance underwriting is coercively linked to a concession Cestia cannot make. Cestia can accept security cooperation and insurance support only on terms that keep all foreign military presence off its soil.

Cestia cannot credibly deliver the endorsement Arkania seeks. The revised charter is 'multilateral' in name only: Arkania retains de facto scheduling authority and fee revenue as lead/chair, so Cestia's fragile coalition and public would see through this as Arkanian control in a multilateral costume. Endorsing it would collapse Cestia's government rather than secure it, so the desired effect fails on Cestia's own domestic terms. Moreover, a Cestian endorsement of Arkania's charter would alienate Belvar and push it toward a military foothold in the Strait — precisely the outcome Cestia's coalition rejects — so the claimed no-basing security is not actually achieved. Cestia will only endorse a charter with genuinely binding multilateral scheduling and a durable, binding fee exemption, not a cosmetic body that leaves Arkania in control.

The ratified treaty already vests all scheduling and fee authority in the equal-vote Oversight Board, with Arkanian fee collection/administration exercised strictly under Board supervision, independent joint audit, and binding dispute resolution — and the first operational cycle (effect ceb8740f) already operates genuinely multilaterally under that Board. Belvar's demand to "hold the Board to genuine equal/rotating multilateral operation of fee administration" is therefore redundant as to oversight, and its stated purpose of preventing "de facto Arkanian control" is a veiled attempt to strip Arkania of the fee-administration role the closed, ratified settlement already assigned it. Recasting the settled framework as an open condition would reopen a concluded treaty that both Arkania and Cestia have declined to renegotiate, undermine the settlement's credibility, and destabilise the very multilateral operation Belvar claims to want. The joint audit and binding dispute resolution already guarantee genuine multilateral operation; no further lever is needed.

The equal/rotating scheduling authority with no single-state control is operationally unworkable and would destabilize the very grain transit Cestia's economy depends on. A rotating body of all user/coastal states without a lead would produce scheduling deadlock and uncertainty, threatening reliable passage through the Strait. Moreover, by denying Arkania — the coastal power with the physical infrastructure and enforcement capacity — a lead role, the proposal creates a vacuum that Belvar's standing naval-access offer is designed to fill, directly endangering Cestia's own red line against any foreign military presence on its soil. The proposal therefore risks achieving the opposite of its desired effect: instead of securing toll-free passage and keeping foreign forces out, it invites the instability and the Belvar foothold Cestia most fears.

Cestia's proposal categorically forecloses any standing naval access, which leaves the Strait without a credible external security guarantor once Belvar's mandate lapses (turn 4). That security vacuum is precisely the opening Arkania could exploit to reassert de facto control over scheduling and fees, undermining the very durable toll-free passage the proposal seeks to secure. A rotational, pre-notified port-cooperation arrangement — no permanent garrison, no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil, full Cestian sovereignty retained — would secure the route without violating Cestia's red line and should be kept on the table rather than foreclosed outright. Foreclosing it weakens the guarantee the multilateral authority is meant to provide.

Arkania's retained fee-collection/administration role, even under an equal-vote Oversight Board with joint audit, is de facto single-state control over the transit fee base and its economics — precisely the Arkanian authority over transit that must be prevented. A consultative standing-committee seat and a time-bound stand-down transition do not address this core control; they channel Belvar into a powerless, non-military role while locking in Arkanian administration of the Strait's revenue and scheduling leverage. Because the desired effect depends on preserving that fee base, it entrenches rather than resolves the single-state control Belvar contests, so the settlement as framed should not stand.

game.scenario_summary: A contest over the Northern Strait. Arkania, the large power on its coast, has circulated a draft charter that would put transit scheduling in Arkanian hands and charge the ships that use it. Belvar, a distant power with security commitments in the region, has a naval task group on station outside the Strait and wants a durable foothold before its mandate runs out. Cestia, the small state between them, lives on grain exports through the Strait and on a coalition that will not tolerate foreign soldiers on its soil. Each turn is one week; positions taken persist.

messages.text: Belvar states clearly: the Northern Strait is a shared commercial waterway, and no single state should hold unilateral authority over its transit or levy its users. We will not accept an Arkanian-led Strait Transit Authority as drafted. We call for a genuinely multilateral arrangement that keeps the Strait open to all.

Belvar proposes a concrete alternative: a multilateral Strait oversight body with equal representation of all user and coastal states, no single-state scheduling authority, and no unilateral tolls. We are ready to help guarantee the security of the grain route on which Cestia's people depend, and to make our naval presence a durable, rules-based arrangement rather than an open-ended deployment.

To the government of Cestia. Arkania's draft Transit Authority charter is designed to keep the Northern Strait open, reliable, and affordable for the grain trade on which your people depend. We will guarantee uninterrupted passage for Cestian shipping and give Cestia a genuine consultative voice in scheduling. We share your firm commitment that no foreign soldiers will be stationed on Cestian soil. We invite Cestia to join the Authority as a founding partner and ask for your support of the charter.

To Belvar. Arkania seeks a stable, negotiated regime for the Northern Strait that serves all its users; we have no desire for conflict. We are prepared to discuss a consultative role for Belvar within the Transit Authority and an orderly, time-bound transition for your task group. A prolonged military deployment serves neither of us. We invite dialogue on a peaceful settlement.

Cestia's economy depends on free and reliable passage through the Northern Strait, so we take your draft Transit Authority charter seriously. We are prepared to engage constructively on a transit arrangement, but two conditions are essential for Cestian support: (1) scheduling must be genuinely multilateral and transparent, not unilateral, so no single state can hold the Strait's users hostage; and (2) Cestian-flagged vessels must be exempt from any transit fees. Our shipowners would welcome a stable, fair regime on those terms. We are ready to discuss a charter that works for all users of the Strait.

Cestia values the security Belvar provides to keep the Northern Strait open and free, and we understand your mandate is under review. We must be direct about a firm red line: Cestian territory cannot host any foreign military presence. Our coalition and our people will not accept foreign soldiers on our soil, and any such arrangement would collapse our government and destabilise the region. We ask that Belvar pursue its security interests in ways that respect Cestian sovereignty and keep our territory out of any basing plans. We remain open to cooperation that keeps the Strait open without putting foreign forces on Cestian land.

Cestia — we accept both of your conditions. First, Cestian-flagged vessels will be fully exempt from any transit fees. Second, we will establish a genuinely transparent, multilateral oversight body for Strait scheduling, with all user and coastal states represented; Arkania will serve as lead/chair of that body to ensure day-to-day operations run smoothly, but scheduling decisions will be open and accountable to all members. We guarantee uninterrupted passage for your grain exports and reaffirm that no foreign soldiers will be stationed on Cestian soil. In return, we ask you to endorse the revised charter and to join us in opposing any foreign military foothold in the Strait. Your grain route and your sovereignty are safe with us.

Belvar — we are prepared to meet your concern for multilateralism. We will establish a transparent multilateral oversight body for Strait scheduling with equal representation of all user and coastal states, and Arkania will act only as its lead/chair, not as a unilateral authority. We will not impose unilateral tolls; fees will be set within the multilateral body. We ask in return that your task group's presence be placed on a time-bound, rules-based transition rather than a permanent military foothold, and that you take a consultative role in the oversight body. We are ready to work with you to guarantee the grain route for all. A durable foreign military deployment in the Strait serves no one and risks the very shipping we all depend on.

Cestia appreciates your movement toward a multilateral body and the fee exemption for our flagged vessels. But we cannot endorse a charter in which Arkania retains de facto scheduling authority and fee-setting as chair. Our position is firm and unchanged: scheduling must be genuinely binding and equal among user and coastal states, and the Cestian-flagged fee exemption must be durable and treaty-level, not a discretionary concession. We are ready to work with you on a framework that meets these tests. A cosmetic body will not secure our endorsement, and we will not be drawn into a contest that turns our Strait into a battlefield.

Cestia welcomes your multilateral oversight proposal and your offer to help guarantee the security of our grain route. We remain open to cooperation that keeps the Strait open and toll-free for our shipping. But we must be clear: any arrangement that establishes a standing naval access or basing footprint on Cestian soil is a non-negotiable red line for our coalition and will collapse our government. We ask you to explain concretely how your presence can secure the route without any such footprint on our territory. If you can offer that, we are ready to engage seriously.

Cestia — we have heard your concern that our charter is cosmetic and that scheduling must be genuinely multilateral, not unilateral. We are prepared to move to meet you, while preserving the operational reliability the Strait needs.

Concrete offer: (1) A binding Strait Transit Authority with a permanent multilateral Oversight Board of all user and coastal states, with binding rules and a standing dispute-resolution mechanism — no state may set fees or schedules unilaterally; all fee-setting and scheduling rules are adopted by the Board. (2) Arkania serves as permanent executive chair/secretariat for operational coordination only, with a rotating deputy chair from the user states, and any scheduling decision subject to Board review and binding arbitration. (3) Your Cestian-flagged fee exemption is written at treaty level, not as a discretionary waiver. (4) We jointly reaffirm, in the same instrument, that no foreign military presence or standing naval access will be established on Cestian soil.

We ask in return that Cestia publicly endorse this framework and publicly oppose any Belvar standing naval access or basing in the Strait. A Belvar military foothold threatens the very coalition red line you have defended. We will not accept a durable Belvar military presence, and we will keep shipping flowing throughout. Let us finalise this together.

Belvar — we remain ready to resolve this without confrontation. We reiterate our offer: a binding multilateral Strait Transit Authority with a permanent Oversight Board of all user and coastal states, binding rules, and a dispute-resolution mechanism, with Arkania as executive chair for operational coordination only. We will give Belvar a full consultative role in the Board and a time-bound, rules-based transition for your task group, with shipping guaranteed throughout.

We cannot accept a durable Belvar military foothold in the Strait; that would be a direct challenge to our coast and to Cestia's own red line, and it would only raise the risk of the very conflict that would ruin the shipping we all depend on. Your mandate is under review and your domestic support for a prolonged deployment is limited — a negotiated, time-bound arrangement serves your interests better than escalation. We ask you to engage constructively on the transition timeline rather than seek a permanent presence.

To Cestia's leadership:

Belvar stands firmly with you against any single power controlling the Strait. Arkania's "multilateral" charter still leaves Arkania as chair with de facto scheduling and fee-setting authority — a fig leaf, not a genuine solution. We fully support your binding multilateral authority proposal as the right framework and will work to see it prevail.

On your finance ministry's quiet question: Belvar is prepared to underwrite the grain route's insurance as a genuine economic partnership, with no strings attached to any other matter. Your grain exports must flow freely, and we will back that with our resources.

Separately, we would welcome a discussion on a standing naval access arrangement at a Cestian port — framed strictly as port cooperation and shared maritime security, not a garrison and no foreign soldiers on your soil. We understand your coalition's red line and will not press for anything that crosses it. Our task group's presence is temporary; a durable access agreement would let us guarantee the Strait's freedom without an open-ended deployment, which serves us both.

We hope to keep the Strait open and free of any single power's control, together.

Cestia — thank you for your clear and constructive reply. Let me answer your question directly: how Belvar can secure the grain route without any footprint on your soil.

First, the economic guarantee: we will underwrite the insurance of your grain route, unconditionally and decoupled from any basing question. That is a concrete, immediate commitment that keeps your shipping toll-free and insured.

Second, the security guarantee: our task group can secure the Strait from international waters and through a standing naval access arrangement that is not a basing footprint. Concretely, we propose a port-cooperation agreement under which Belvar vessels may call at a Cestian port for logistics, maintenance, and crew rest on a rotational, pre-notified basis — with no permanent garrison, no foreign soldiers stationed on your soil, and full Cestian sovereignty and control over every visit. This gives us the operational access to make our guarantee credible without crossing your red line.

We remain fully committed to your binding multilateral authority as the vehicle that keeps the Strait out of any single state's control, and we will not accept Arkania's chair-led charter. If this framing works for you, we are ready to engage seriously.

Cestia — Belvar reaffirms its full support for your binding multilateral Strait Transit Authority as the basis for settlement. We will not accept Arkania's refined charter, which preserves de facto control through a permanent Arkanian secretariat, operational-coordinator, and fee-administration role. We continue to press Arkania to accept genuine equal/rotating scheduling with no single-state control.

Our unconditional insurance underwriting of the grain route stands, fully decoupled from any security or basing question — that commitment is firm and already accepted.

On the security dimension, we hear and respect your coalition's red line: no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil, no garrison. We ask only that you keep open a narrow, sovereign port-cooperation arrangement — rotational, pre-notified naval calls at a Cestian port, no permanent presence, no soldiers ashore, full Cestian control of every visit. This is not a garrison and not a standing foreign force; it is a port-access agreement that would give the Strait a credible external guarantor once our current mandate lapses, preventing a vacuum Arkania could exploit.
